oewn-02389828-v.learner: to ask someone to come to your house.
examples: Lady Catherine, with great condescension, wished them a good journey, and invited them to come to Hunsford again next year
They will then join his regiment, unless they are first invited to Longbourn

oewn-01811496-v.learner: to make someone want something by being attractive or welcoming.
examples: his manners, though well bred, were not inviting
The cool water of the pool invited us on that hot afternoon.

oewn-00795242-v.learner: to ask someone in a friendly way to do something.
examples: Her prudent mother, occupied by the same ideas, forbore to invite him to sit by herself.
He invited her to tell the whole story from the beginning.

oewn-00164054-n.learner: the act of meaning to do something; a choice of the will that you mean to carry out.
examples: her father had not the smallest intention of yielding
though without seeming to have any intention of speaking

oewn-05991037-n.learner: the result you are hoping for, which shapes what you plan to do.
examples: "We acted with the best intentions."
Thus much for my general intention in favour of matrimony

oewn-05991605-n.learner: what a person aims at in the matter of asking someone to marry them; the word is usually plural.
examples: Her father wished to know whether the young man's intentions were honourable.

oewn-15295994-n.learner: a stretch of time in which something stops for a while.
examples: After a pause of some minutes, she addressed him a second time
She found that she was to receive no other answer; and, after a short pause, added

oewn-01064741-n.learner: a short time in which nothing is being done.
examples: Darcy only smiled; and the general pause which ensued made Elizabeth tremble
after an awkward pause, they returned to the rest of the family

oewn-00120034-r.learner: however; the word is put after the words it belongs with, not before them.
examples: The room was small. It was warm, though.
I would rather not go. I will come if you need me, though.

oewn-03239009-n.learner: a picture of shapes or things made with lines on a surface.
examples: She hung a drawing of the old house above the fireplace.

oewn-07016235-n.learner: a picture made by hand and printed in a book, a magazine, or a newspaper.
examples: The drawing on page ten shows how the engine works.

oewn-00937756-n.learner: the making of pictures or diagrams as an art.
examples: She spent the winter studying drawing and music.
something has occurred of a most unexpected and serious nature
We may as well wait, perhaps, till the circumstance occurs

oewn-00725311-v.learner: to come into your mind as a thought.
examples: I am glad it occurred to me to mention it
though it had not occurred to me before

oewn-02618403-v.learner: to be found to exist somewhere.
examples: These birds occur only on the islands in the south.

oewn-13832132-n.learner: a small part of something that you can look at on its own, apart from the whole.
examples: "Could Colonel Forster repeat the particulars of Lydia's note to his wife?"
The particulars I reserve till we meet.

oewn-05826326-n.learner: a fact about one part of something rather than about the whole.
examples: It is safer not to argue from the particular to the general.

oewn-06763856-n.learner: in logic, a statement that says something about some members of a group but not about all of them.
examples: "Some birds cannot fly" is a particular, since it says nothing about the rest.

oewn-01817851-v.learner: to feel happy or full of joy.

his friends may well rejoice in his having met with one of the very few sensible women

oewn-00859605-v.learner: to show great joy in what you say or do.
examples: When the war ended the whole town rejoiced in the streets.

oewn-01827320-v.learner: to be filled with joy so great that you can hardly contain it.
examples: They rejoiced beyond all measure when the child was found alive.

oewn-00746935-n.learner: ways of acting that are wrong in a moral way.
examples: there is, I believe, in every disposition a tendency to some particular evil, a natural defect

connotation.why: names conduct as morally condemnable rather than merely wrong

oewn-04859319-n.learner: the quality of being morally wrong, either in what is believed or in what is done.
examples: She could not believe there was so much evil in one man.

connotation.why: condemns what it names rather than simply describing wrongness

oewn-05944010-n.learner: something that you bring back into your mind.

The recollection of what I then said, of my conduct, my manners, my expressions during the whole of it, is now inexpressibly painful to me.

oewn-05769556-n.learner: the act of remembering, especially getting something back into your mind by an effort of thought.
examples: Darcy, after a few moments' recollection, was not sorry for it
with a moment's recollection, and a returning smile, replied

oewn-05769915-n.learner: the power to bring back to mind things that happened before.
